text: Hello, and welcome to our project introduction. Over the next eight minutes, we will take a complete tour of EduNova — a modern Learning Management System built by Team EduNova. First, we will explore every feature through the eyes of its three kinds of users. Then we will go under the hood: the architecture, the programming technologies, the data model, the automated test suites, and the Git and C I C D workflow that holds the whole project together.

EduNova is a full stack web application for online learning, delivered in two releases. The first release covered the core platform: secure registration and login, a public course catalogue, enrolments, lesson tracking, grading, and an administrator console. The second release hardened the project around engineering practice: a front-end unit test suite, browser level end to end tests with Cypress, a version controlled repository with a proper branching workflow, and a continuous integration pipeline that builds and tests every change automatically. Everything you are about to see is real, running code — no mock-ups.

Our tour starts at the course catalogue — the front door of the platform. Anyone can browse published courses without an account. The catalogue supports live search, category filters, difficulty levels and pagination, and every filter is synced into the U R L, so any view can be shared as a simple link. Each course card shows its cover image, level, price and the instructor behind it. Watch how typing in the search box filters the results instantly, without reloading the page.

Clicking a card opens the course detail page. The curriculum is displayed as an ordered list of lessons, each with its duration and summary. A student can enrol in a single click. Once enrolled, the page switches into learning mode: every lesson gets a checkbox, and ticking one sends an update through the REST API, which recalculates progress on the server. When the last lesson is completed, the enrolment is automatically marked as finished — and the progress bar at the top updates live. Scrolling down reveals the full instructor profile and the course statistics.

Authentication is token based and fully stateless. New users register with a name, an email and a password — passwords are hashed with bcrypt before they ever touch the database, so plain text is never stored. On login, the server signs a JSON Web Token that expires after seven days. The client keeps this token in local storage and attaches it to every request. On the server, middleware verifies the signature and the expiry before any controller runs, and invalid or missing tokens are rejected with a structured error response.

After signing in, students land on My Learning — their personal dashboard. It shows statistics at a glance: total enrolments, courses in progress, completed courses, and average progress. Every enrolment card carries a progress bar, and once an instructor has graded it, the final score appears right there. Behind these screens sits a role system with three levels — student, instructor and administrator — enforced by role based authorization middleware on the server, plus ownership checks so instructors can only ever manage their own courses.

Instructors get a dedicated teaching dashboard. From here they publish or unpublish a course with one click, and the change becomes visible in the public catalogue immediately. The New Course form validates every field against server-side rules. Inside the course editor, instructors manage an ordered list of lessons, reorder them, and update the course settings. The Roster tab lists every enrolled student, where grades can be submitted inline — and grading an enrolment marks it as completed on the student's dashboard.

Finally, administrators manage the whole user base from one table: searching by name or email, filtering by role, creating and editing accounts, resetting passwords, and deleting users — all protected by guard rails, such as being unable to delete your own account. Every one of these actions passes through the same validation and permission checks you saw earlier.

Let's go under the hood. Every request in EduNova follows the same journey. The React client sends a fetch call — with the JSON Web Token attached — through the Vite development proxy to Express, which removes C O R S friction entirely during development. Express middleware then applies security headers, request rate limiting, authentication, and role checks. The controller runs the business logic through Mongoose models, MongoDB persists the data with proper indexes, and a consistent JSON envelope — success or error — flows back to the client. Because this contract is uniform, every layer can be tested in isolation.

Now, the programming technologies. On the front end: React eighteen with functional components and hooks, Vite as the build tool with instant hot module replacement, Tailwind C S S for utility-first styling, React Router for navigation, and the Context API for global state such as the session and toast notifications. On the back end: Node dot js and Express, structured in the Model View Controller pattern — Mongoose models for the data, controllers for the business logic, routes for the U R L mapping, and dedicated middleware for cross-cutting concerns. The whole codebase is modern JavaScript — E S modules on the client, CommonJS on the server.

The database is MongoDB, organised into four collections: users, courses, lessons, and enrollments. Mongoose schemas define every field with types, defaults, enumerations and validators, and unique indexes guarantee that no two accounts share an email, and no course code is duplicated. Relationships are modelled with references — an enrolment points at its student and its course, a lesson belongs to its course — and deletions cascade automatically, so removing a course cleans up its lessons and enrolments in one safe operation.

Security is layered. Passwords are hashed with bcrypt using per-user salts. JSON Web Tokens carry the identity and the role, expire after seven days, and are verified on every protected route. Login is rate limited to slow down brute force attempts, Helmet sets strict security headers on every response, and all input is validated before it ever reaches a model. Authorization is enforced in two dimensions: what your role allows, and what you own — so even a valid instructor token cannot touch another instructor's course.

Quality is verified by three automated suites. The API is covered by fifty nine tests written with Mocha, Chai and Supertest, running the real Express stack against a dedicated test database — every C R U D path, plus authentication, permissions, validation and conflict cases. The front end adds twenty one unit tests built with Vitest and React Testing Library. And Cypress drives ten end to end scenarios through a real browser — registration, login, catalogue filtering, and a complete course C R U D journey performed by an instructor — with every run recorded to video and captured in screenshots as submission evidence.

The project is fully version controlled with Git, following a clean branching workflow: features are developed on a dedicated branch, committed, reviewed, and then merged back into the main branch — and the change goes live the moment the page reloads, as our before and after screenshots prove. On every push, a GitHub Actions pipeline installs the dependencies, starts a real MongoDB service, runs the API test suite and the front-end unit tests, builds the client, and executes the Cypress suite. A red build means the change never ships.

That's EduNova: a complete learning platform — catalogue, enrolments, lessons, grading and administration — backed by React, Tailwind, Node, Express and MongoDB, verified by automated tests, and delivered through a disciplined Git and C I C D workflow. All documentation, test evidence and recordings are included in the submission package. Thank you for watching.
